title: 2 Monster Stocks to Hold for the Next 10 Years

The best stocks don't just beat the market for a year or two. They compound wealth for a decade or more, and that kind of return almost always traces back to a business that keeps growing its customer base, revenue, and profits.

MercadoLibre (NASDAQ:MELI) and Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN) have both delivered monster returns, and their businesses are still growing, making them quality stocks to hold for 10 years.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

1. MercadoLibre

A $10,000 investment in MercadoLibre 10 years ago would be worth about $94,000 today, a roughly 25% annualized return. However, the stock trades more than 40% below its June 2025 high because profits have stalled.

That is a deliberate choice, as management is prioritizing investments to strengthen the business for long-term growth. Management has lowered Brazil's free-shipping threshold several times since 2017, while ramping up credit card issuance and expanding fulfillment space nearly 20% last quarter.

It's short-term pain for long-term gain. Operating margin fell to 6.3% from 9.8% a year ago, even as revenue climbed 45% year over year. On the Nov. 4, 2026, earnings call, CEO Ariel Szarfsztejn said the company has "accepted a lower margin" to deepen customer relationships.

Those relationships are showing up in other metrics. Gross merchandise volume (GMV) rose 38% to $23 billion, unique active buyers grew 22% to 93.9 million, and purchase frequency hit a record.

The risk is that competition from Shopee and others keeps profits down longer than investors expect. Still, the economics are improving. Brazil's cost per shipment is down 14% since Q1 2025, and high-margin advertising grew 58%.

Analysts expect earnings per share (EPS) to jump 45% to $52.62 in 2027, according to Yahoo! Finance. At $1,491 as of Nov. 13, 2026, the stock trades at 28 times that estimate. That's a fair valuation for a quality e-commerce stock with excellent long-term growth prospects.

Image source: Getty Images.

2. Amazon

A $10,000 investment in Amazon 10 years ago would be worth about $70,000 today, a roughly 22% annualized return. The engine behind those gains is growth in operating income, which reached $104 billion over the past year, up 37% year over year, excluding foreign currency effects.

Amazon Web Services (AWS) is a fast-growing, high-margin business, with revenue up 39% to $46 billion last quarter, and a backlog of $578 billion. CEO Andy Jassy expects AWS to grow more than 40% in both 2027 and 2028. Amazon also plans to sell its Trainium AI chips outside AWS starting late 2027.

Today's big story: Could Nvidia Stock Fall 50%? Follow The Cash

Coupang (CPNG) stock fell 5.5% on Monday, November 16, 2026, while the S&P 500 lost 1.9%. The company issued no announcements, earnings reports or filings, and the drop came on a day the Nasdaq Composite fell 2.5%. What was moving the market that Monday, and where does Coupang fit in it?

What Happened In The Market On November 16?

Chip stocks fell, with AMD and Intel sliding ahead of two big tests for the AI trade: Nvidia's results on Tuesday and Anthropic's expected trading debut on Thursday.

Amazon had troubles of its own. It fell 3.3% on a new AI chip export rule and a Vulcan rocket failure that destroyed 40 of its Leo satellites. Amazon and Coupang are both broadline retailers that sell goods online. Coupang sells in South Korea and in Taiwan, where it runs its own last mile network. In South Korea, it is the dominant force in logistics.

Did Coupang Fall With Other Broadline Retailers?

Coupang fell with its group, but much further. Six of the eight other broadline retailers worth $2 billion or more also fell. Across all eight, the median move was a 1.3% drop, and none of them fell 5% or more. The consumer discretionary sector fund XLY lost 1.5%.

Etsy, one of Coupang's peers, fell 4.5%, while Walmart rose 0.2%. Coupang posted a larger drop than any peer, following earlier falls of 2.1% on November 11 and 4.4% on November 12.

Coupang Stock Sits Near Its One-Year Low

Coupang stock has seen three falls at least this large in the prior 365 days. Its last move this large was a 12.0% gain on November 4. That was the day after its third-quarter earnings call.

Over the past twelve months the stock lost 49.7%, while the S&P 500 returned 11.4%. Monday's close of $14.35 sits near the stock's lowest close of the past year, $13.75 on September 28, 2026. Coupang's market value is now 0.71 times its yearly sales. For the S&P 500, that ratio is 3.2.

Coupang next reports its fourth quarter of fiscal 2026. The figure to watch is the adjusted EBITDA margin of its Product Commerce segment, which management put at 4.6% for the third quarter and said it believes was the low point.

Coupang said nothing on Monday and still fell further than any of its eight sub-industry peers with a market value of $2 billion or more. Being ready for days like that matters more than trying to call them.

Booking Holdings vs. MercadoLibre: Which Consumer Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?

Investors often choose between proven global leaders and high-growth regional powerhouses. Deciding between Booking Holdings Inc. (NASDAQ:BKNG) and MercadoLibre Inc. (NASDAQ:MELI) requires weighing stable profitability against an expanding digital ecosystem in Latin America.

Booking serves the global travel market through its massive network of accommodations and flight options. MercadoLibre dominates Latin American e-commerce and digital payments, functioning as both a retailer and a bank. While both companies operate in the consumer discretionary space, they offer very different risk-reward profiles for long-term investors looking toward 2027.

The case for Booking Holdings

Booking operates a massive network of consumer-facing brands, including Booking.com, Priceline, Agoda, and OpenTable. The company focuses on its "connected trip" strategy, which aims to integrate accommodations, flights, and rental cars into a single, seamless itinerary for travelers. By managing nearly 4.7 million accommodation properties, it relies on a broad network of travel service providers that typically operate on non-exclusive terms.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached about $28.1 billion, representing roughly 8% growth compared to the prior year. The company reported net income of approximately $7.2 billion, reflecting a net margin of about 25.5%. This performance demonstrates the company's ability to generate significant profit while expanding its presence in the international travel market.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the company carries a negative debt-to-equity ratio of roughly -3.5x, indicating that its total liabilities exceed shareholder equity. The debt-to-equity ratio, which compares total debt to the equity held by shareholders, measures how a business balances its obligations against its assets. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, free cash flow, which is cash flow from operations minus capital expenditures, was about $9.1 billion.

The case for MercadoLibre

MercadoLibre operates the leading commerce and fintech ecosystem in Latin America, driven by the Mercado Libre marketplace and its Mercado Pago payment platform. As a leader among consumer discretionary stocks in its region, it relies on a vast network of third-party sellers and logistics partners. Its integrated strategy combines retail, lending, and asset management to serve over 136 million unique buyers.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached about $38.5 billion, marking about 47% growth over the previous period. The company reported net income of approximately $1.9 billion, resulting in a net margin of roughly 4.9%. This rapid top-line expansion highlights the scaling nature of its integrated digital services across major markets like Brazil and Mexico.

Analysts expect sales to grow another 27% next year. That would be faster than every Consumer Discretionary company worth more than $50 billion except MercadoLibre. Yet 14 of those 21 companies cost more than Carvana per dollar of sales, from Amazon to McDonald's. Carvana's market value is 2.9 times its sales. Three things explain that low price: the yardstick, the stock's fall in 2022, and car loans.

Is Carvana Really Cheap?

Only per dollar of sales. Selling a car brings in a lot of money but leaves a thin profit. Over the last 12 months, Carvana kept 19 cents per dollar of sales after the cost of the cars. It kept 8.7 cents of operating profit, what is left after all running costs. McDonald's kept 46.1 cents of operating profit per dollar.

Key Takeaways

Stanley Druckenmiller's Duquesne Family Office added 45% to its Sea stake in the third quarter, and the stock has fallen 26% since Sept. 30.

Big funds also bought Alibaba, Coupang and MercadoLibre in the quarter, and all but Coupang have fallen since.

Sea's revenue grew 43% last quarter, but its profit came in below expectations as it spent on AI and fought rivals for share.

At about 17x forward earnings, with analysts' average target 81% above the price, Sea looks like the best buy of the four.

Stanley Druckenmiller's Duquesne Family Office added 45% more shares of Sea (SE:NYSE) in the third quarter, according to its 13F for the quarter ended Sept. 30, filed Nov. 16. Sea's stock is down 26% since then.

He had plenty of company. Big funds also bought Alibaba (BABA:NYSE), Coupang (CPNG:NYSE) and MercadoLibre (MELI:NASDAQ) in the quarter. Three of the four stocks are lower since then, and Sea, Alibaba and Coupang are each about half below their 52-week highs.

Druckenmiller wasn't the biggest buyer of Sea

Duquesne held 1.59 million Sea shares worth $155 million on Sept. 30. That made Sea its seventh-biggest position, at 3.7% of the $4.15 billion of US stocks its 13F holds.

Causeway Capital Management, a $62 billion firm, made a much bigger bet. It bought 9.19 million new shares worth $894 million, and Sea became 10.0% of its 13F stocks and its third-biggest holding. Dan Sundheim's D1 Capital added 118% to its stake, and Lone Pine Capital added 490%.

Not everyone bought. Chase Coleman's Tiger Global cut its stake 43%. Of the big funds that have filed for the quarter, nine bought Sea or added 20% or more, and four sold out or cut 20% or more. A 13F only shows what a fund held on Sept. 30, so the 26% drop is measured from the quarter-end price, and we don't know what any of these funds paid.

Sea reported its third quarter on Nov. 10. Revenue rose 43% to $8.6 billion. Shopee, its e-commerce business, had its most profitable quarter ever, with adjusted EBITDA up 45% to $269 million.

But group adjusted EBITDA of $931 million fell short of the $990 million analysts expected, and Bloomberg put the miss down to higher AI spending and tougher e-commerce competition. Garena's bookings grew just 5.9%. Monee's revenue grew 64% while its adjusted EBITDA rose only 15.5%, as its loan book grew 60% to $12.6 billion. The board did add $1 billion to Sea's buyback.

Can MercadoLibre's GMV Growth Fuel Long-Term Earnings Gains?
Sumit Singh
Mon, November 16, 2026 at 7:07 AM PST 4 min read
MELI
AMZN
SE
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

MercadoLibre, Inc. MELI continues to build momentum in Latin America's e-commerce market, supported by higher purchase frequency, expanding customer engagement and improving logistics efficiency. In third-quarter 2026, gross merchandise volume (GMV) reached $22.8 billion, increasing 38% year over year on a reported basis and 33% on an FX-neutral basis, while items sold rose 36% to 867 million. Unique active buyers increased approximately 22.3% to 93.9 million, highlighting sustained marketplace adoption and deeper customer engagement.

Brazil remains a major growth driver, with FX-neutral GMV advancing 36% and items sold rising 45%. The company's lower free-shipping threshold continues to encourage more frequent purchases, with items per buyer increasing 16% year over year. Management also reported stronger retention among customer cohorts acquired after the threshold reduction. However, smaller baskets and more free shipments have reduced shipping revenue per shipment. As a result, net shipping margin as a percentage of GMV has declined approximately 200 basis points since first-quarter 2025.

Meanwhile, Brazil's cost per shipment fell 5% year over year in local currency and 14% compared with first-quarter 2025, reflecting improving logistics efficiency. In September, free and slow shipments in the R$19-R$79 price range became variable contribution-positive for the first time. MercadoLibre is also expanding its logistics capabilities, having opened 13 Metro fulfillment centers over the past 12 months and more than doubled the number of sorters and robots across its network. Management expects higher shipment density, automation and better network utilization to drive further cost improvements.

Still, stronger GMV growth has yet to translate fully into operating profitability. Third-quarter operating income declined 6% year over year to $676 million, while the operating margin reached 6.3%, down 40 basis points sequentially. Net shipping costs created a 60-basis-point margin headwind, reflecting increased free shipping, higher energy expenses and additional fulfillment capacity. Increased affiliate marketing investments in Brazil also pressured margins. Nevertheless, net income rose 6% to $448 million, supported by a lower tax rate and reduced foreign-exchange losses.

Management expects improving logistics productivity and greater operating scale to gradually reduce shipping costs relative to business volumes. MercadoLibre's ability to sustain purchase frequency while lowering fulfillment costs remains central to translating marketplace growth into stronger long-term earnings.

What Happened?

MercadoLibre (MELI) stock declined approximately 20% from its October 5 closing price of $1,860.61 to $1,490.24 on November 10, after hitting a new 52-week low on November 5.

The decline reflects two concerns: political uncertainty in Brazil and weaker-than-expected profitability despite strong revenue growth.

Brazil's October 25 presidential runoff delivered another term for Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, who defeated Flávio Bolsonaro after trailing him in the first round.

MercadoLibre shares fell approximately 8% on October 26 as investors reassessed Brazil's economic outlook, currency risks, and consumer spending conditions.

Brazil generated approximately $15.2 billion of MercadoLibre's $28.9 billion in 2025 revenue, making it the company's largest market.

However, the company's third-quarter earnings report created a more immediate concern.

According to MercadoLibre's third-quarter financial results, revenue and financial income increased 45% year over year to $10.75 billion, but reported earnings of $8.83 per share fell short of the $9.27 consensus estimate cited in the initial research brief.

Operating margin declined to 6.3% from approximately 9.8% a year earlier, reflecting higher shipping expenses, expanded fulfillment capacity, and increased marketing spending in Brazil.

In its third-quarter shareholder letter, management described the pressure on shipping margins as "the price of the habit we set out to build."

The strategy is producing results. Items sold in Brazil increased more than 40% year over year for the fifth consecutive quarter, while MercadoLibre gained market share across its three largest markets.

Its lower free-shipping threshold also encouraged smaller purchases, initially putting pressure on shipping economics.

By September, Brazilian orders valued between R$19 and R$79 that qualified for free or slower delivery became variable contribution-positive for the first time, suggesting higher order volumes are beginning to improve shipping economics.
